episode_narrative: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
event_narrative: An NWS storm survey team confirmed an EF-0 with peak winds of 85 mph touched down on the southern side of Thibodaux at 12:45am on February 15th. An trailer RV was partially flipped off of Talbot Ave as the tornado moved to the east-southeast. The tornado then reach peak strength as it impacted Tabernacle Pentecostal Church. Here, the tornado lifted a significant portion of the roof of the church, displacing it to the east. The wood framing of the roofing had evidence of rotting, so the lower bound for that damage was used in this case. The tornado slightly weakened as it moved east-southeast where minimal damage was found until it reached Percy Brown Rd where multiple large branches were snapped along it. The tornado remained very weak as it continued to the east-southeast where the next notable damage came on Crossing North St where a backyard awning was uplifted. As the tornado moved to the east-northeast, vegetation damage was noted on high-resolution imagery north of Rousseau where the tornado appeared to have lifted though additional analysis will be needed to determine the end point over inaccessible areas.

event_narrative: An EF-1 tornado touched down along Ancil Cox Road on the southwest side of Centreville near Griffin Lane. A few trees were downed here, with at least one of them taking down a powerline. The tornado tracked northeast, generally paralleling Ancil Cox Road until reaching the intersection with Old Highway 33. The most significant damage occurred near this intersection, where approximately a dozen trees were uprooted or snapped which supports the 90 mph wind rating. Beyond this point, the tornado continued northeastward producing sporadic tree and limb damage along its path. The final accessible point of the tornado���s track was near Centerville Academy. Minor damage was observed on campus, including a downed light pole, partial roof uplift on a metal building, and a baseball pitching backstop that was thrown approximately 250 feet into a chain-link fence. The tornado continued northeast beyond Lower Centreville Rd where additional minor tree damage was identified. The tornado evidently lifted over inaccessible areas to the survey team prior to reaching Hwy 48.

episode_narrative: Severe drought conditions (D2���D3) developed and intensified across portions of the New Orleans/Baton Rouge WFO area during February 2026, driven by persistent precipitation deficits and limited meaningful rainfall events. Early in the month, only isolated areas of severe drought (D2) were present across the northwestern parts of the region, but conditions steadily worsened as rainfall remained below normal, with precipitation deficits of roughly 2 to 4 inches observed across much of the region by the end of February. As a result, D2 drought expanded significantly across southern and southwestern portions of the forecast area, while pockets of extreme drought (D3) developed, particularly near coastal Louisiana. By late February, over 30 percent of the area was classified in D2 drought and more than 10 percent in D3, reflecting a rapid degradation in soil moisture and hydrologic conditions. The expansion of drought was most pronounced south of the Interstate 10 corridor, while areas farther north experienced more gradual degradation, generally remaining in D0 to D1 conditions.

episode_narrative: A band of heavy snow, coupled with gusty winds and reduced visibility, impacted east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa beginning on the afternoon of February 19, 2026, and continuing into the early morning hours of February 20, 2026. The heaviest band of snow fell generally along a line from Lincoln, NE, to Omaha, NE, to Council Bluffs, IA, with a maximum snowfall of 10.3 inches measured 4 miles southeast of Bennington, Nebraska. Numerous snowfall reports in the 7 to 9-inch range were received across Lancaster, Douglas, Sarpy, Dodge, and Saunders counties in Nebraska, as well as Pottawattamie, Mills, and Harrison counties in Iowa.||The system was forced by a broad trough moving across much of the CONUS, accompanied by a potent shortwave trough that tracked into central Nebraska. As the system took shape, a surface low maintained impressive depth, progressing slowly across northern Kansas before deepening as it pivoted and ejected from northwestern Missouri toward Wisconsin. As the low passed to the south and east, strong height falls, warm air advection, elevated instability, and frontogenesis wrapped along its northern periphery, driving a narrow but potent band of snow into east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Model soundings exhibited steep lapse rates, which supported convective snowband development and impressive snowfall rates across the area. This was coupled with wind gusts in the 25 to 35 mph range, frequently reducing visibility to below one-quarter of a mile in many locations.

episode_narrative: A period of extremely cold temperatures that began in late January spilled into the first week of February amid a cold airmass dominating the bulk of the country. Daytime temperatures for the start of the month struggled to rise above freezing and plummeting to sub-zero values during the overnight hours. Local cooperative observers and CoCoRaHS members recorded low temperatures ranging around minus one to minus five some mornings across southeast Ohio, with one local resident in New Lexington recording a low temperatures of minus seventeen on the morning of February 1st. While temperatures oscillated for the first week of the month in and out of freezing thresholds, strong warm air advection took hold on February 12th, which ended the cold spell. A thirty degree temperature rise was noted for daytime highs from February 9th to the 10th in response to the push of warmer temperatures filtering into the Ohio Valley.||In the midst of these very cold temperatures, a vehicle traveling on East Main Street in Pomeroy veered off the roadway, struck a utility pole, and plunged into the icy Ohio River in Meigs County. The driver was pronounced dead at the scene, but her body was not immediately recovered until the middle of March down river in Greenup County, Kentucky. A young juvenile occupant inside the car was rescued by first responders and transported to a hospital on the evening of the crash with minor injuries.

episode_narrative: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

On the southern fringe of the drought���s extent, D2 intensity persisted in northwestern Parke, northwestern Vigo, and northern Henry counties.||Precipitation throughout February was once again critically low, frequently falling well below 50% of monthly norms. episode_narrative: Eastern Oklahoma experienced only one rainfall event during the month of February. During this mid-month event, rainfall across the region ranged from one hundredth to one tenth of an inch across portions of northeastern Oklahoma to as much as three to four inches across portions of east central and southeastern Oklahoma. The rainfall that fell across eastern Oklahoma in February was below the monthly average amounts for much of the region, with a large portion of northeastern Oklahoma only receiving from one to five percent of monthly average precipitation amounts. These very dry conditions, compounding on several months of dry weather, allowed the drought that developed across portions of the region in January to expand in February. Severe (D2) drought conditions developed across all of Washington, Nowata, Craig, Ottawa, Rogers, Mayes, Delaware, Wagoner, and Cherokee Counties, and developed across portions of Tulsa, Muskogee, Adair, McIntosh, Pittsburg, Pushmataha, and Choctaw Counties. Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed into portions of Choctaw, Ottawa, Delaware, Mayes, Wagoner, Cherokee, Muskogee and Adair Counties during the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

A record-breaking winter storm impacted western Montana as a very cold trough, originating from Siberia, transitioned southeast into the region. This system coincided with an Arctic air mass pushing west toward the Continental Divide. A powerful surface low of 981 millibars broke all-time February sea level pressure records across the Northern Rockies, including a record 985.2 mb at Missoula (previous record 985.5 mb in 1963). The negatively tilted nature of the trough resulted in prolonged heavy snowfall on the morning of the 17th, particularly across northwest Montana. By February 18th, shortwaves embedded in the cyclonic flow produced convective snow showers and squalls overrunning the Arctic boundary in place. This brought isolated flash-freeze and high impact travel to the evening commute.
event_narrative: Snow showers combined with breezy south winds less than 20 mph brought slick conditions and low visibility to the Butte area. These conditions led to multiple injury crashes on I-15 and I-90. Incidents included a crash with injuries just west of Butte on I-90 between 1330MST and 1430MST, and three injury crashes on I-15 just inside Silver Bow County between 1400MST and 1500MST.

episode_narrative: In the days leading up to this event, a strong trough made landfall along the West Coast of the US. Ahead of this system, unusually warm and dry conditions prevailed as high pressure dominated the Intermountain West. The trough began to track inland on the 15th into the 16th, but the high pressure was reluctant to shift east. This led to a tightening up of the pressure gradient between these two features, enhancing an already strong southwesterly upper level jet. Lift began to increase ahead of the trough on the evening of the 16th, with mountain rain and snow showers breaking out over the higher terrain of eastern Utah and western Colorado. This also helped to keep deep mixing ongoing well after sunset, resulting in some of the peak winds occurring between midnight and daybreak on the 17th. In addition, a potent cold front was associated with this system, and was expected to sweep through eastern Utah and western Colorado around daybreak. Ahead of the cold front, the surface pressure gradient tightened substantially and surface winds maxed out. This coincided with the period between midnight and daybreak on the 17th.
event_narrative: Peak gust to 59 mph occurred at 10:10 PM MST 2/16 at the Hole N The Rock mesonet site, south of Moab, UT. An additional gust to 59 mph occurred at the Hole N The Rock site at 1:20 AM MST 2/17, with a gust to 58 mph at the US-191 at MP 104 Flat Iron Utah Department of Transportation site at 3:30 AM MST 2/17. Other gusts at various sensors around the zone ranged from 45 mph to 55 mph during the period of highest winds. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities associated with this high wind event were received.

episode_narrative: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.
event_narrative: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Wilkinson County remained under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions throughout February. Following the initial onset of D2 on November 25, 2025, the county experienced a brief period of mid-winter marginal improvement before conditions degraded back to D2 levels in late January. By the end of February, the county had recorded a total of 10 weeks at or above the D2 threshold, with drought conditions persisting into March.

A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.

episode_narrative: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across the Ozarks but limited precipitation through the month allowed Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to develop across portions of far south central Missouri. Some expansion of drought conditions occurred through the month across portions of southwestern Missouri as well. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
event_narrative: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced continued dry conditions with drought remaining Severe (D2) drought to Moderate (D1) drought in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

episode_narrative: A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Most of these tornadoes were brief, and none were stronger than EF-1, but one serious injury occurred in Crawford County as a result of a tornado. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.
event_narrative: Thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident on I-57 southwest of Watson, resulting in one indirect injury.

An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East Texas through the month of February. Rainfall amounts during February only tallied to 0.50-1.75 inches, which was less than half of the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, extreme (D3) drought had expanded farther southeast from Red River, Franklin, and Titus Counties to start the month into Western Bowie, Morris, and Camp Counties.

A coastal low stationed off the Tidewater of Virginia during the morning to afternoon hours of February 22, 2026 allowed for ample moisture influx from the Atlantic with light snow forming across portions of eastern Pennsylvania. Light snow was mainly observed throughout the morning and afternoon hours with heavier snow beginning during the late evening hours and throughout the morning hours of February 23rd across portions of eastern Pennsylvania. This heavier snow was due to a combination of bombogenesis of the aforementioned area of low pressure and ample frontogenetic forcing that allowed for a heavy band of snowfall to form across portions of south-central Pennsylvania extending into the Susquehanna Valley. Winds associated with the pressure gradient of the rapidly deepening cyclone allowed for gusty winds, generally in the 30 to 40 mph range, across much of eastern Pennsylvania with highest gusts closer to the Atlantic Coast. Slick conditions and gusty winds from this system allowed for multiple accidents across eastern Pennsylvania, including one that resulted in one injury in Lancaster County.

Snowfall totals generally ranged between four to six inches with the multiple reports across eastern portions of the county ranging between five to seven inches of snowfall from this system. Winds associated with this system also knocked down a tree down into power lines that fell onto State Route 216, closing the roadway for multiple hours.

episode_narrative: A strengthening storm system lifted through the Middle Mississippi Valley on the 19th, dragging its warm frontal zone northward through the Midwest, and bringing near-record high temperatures and anomalous dewpoints into central Indiana.  Multiple rounds of severe weather occurred over the region, from early morning large hail in two far-northern zones, covering roads in Warren County, to more organized evening severe weather from rotating supercell thunderstorms.  Through the evening of the 19th, the destabilized atmosphere combined with a stregthening low-level jet stream that progressed eastward into the region, boosting 0-1 km wind shear as high as 300 m2/s2.  A resultant cluster of discrete late-day to evening supercells were focused along the frontal zone, near or south of the Interstate 70 corridor, and produced scattered large hail over 6 counties and isolated wind damage to trees and/or power poles in 4 counties.  ||A stronger supercell with a history of producing two weak tornadoes in Crawford County, Illinois, continued into central Indiana, spawning an EF-0 tornado in Sullivan County, an intense EF-2 just west of Bloomington that caused extensive structural damage to homes, apartments, and airport facilities, and a brief EF-U in Decatur County;  this cell also produced ping-pong ball (1.50-inch diameter) sized hail in Greene and Monroe Counties.

episode_narrative: A winter storm system tracked across the West Coast, North Slope, and Interior Alaska from February 20 through February 25, 2026. The episode began with widespread blizzard conditions impacting the West Coast and North Slope regions, where powerful winds and significant blowing snow reduced visibilities to near zero. As the system pushed inland, it transitioned into a heavy snow event for the Central and Eastern Interior. Notable snowfall reports included thirteen and one-half inches measured northwest of Ester and nearly nine inches reported by storm spotters in the Tanana Valley. Additionally, measurements from the Nenana Snotel indicated a seven-inch snow depth increase over a twenty-four-hour period during the height of the storm. These conditions created hazardous travel and significant impacts to infrastructure across the state. No fatalities or injuries were reported during this episode.
event_narrative: A heavy snow event impacted Eielson Air Force Base and Salcha, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 1027AKST on February 21 through 1159AKST on February 24, 2026. A trained spotter reported eight and eight-tenths inches of snow accumulation between the evening of Sunday, February 22, and 2130AKST on Monday, February 23. During the event, the Eielson Air Force Base Airport (PAEI) reported visibilities as low as one-half mile in heavy snow and freezing fog. The first verifying observation for the heavy snow occurred at 2130AKST on February 23. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

episode_narrative: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
event_narrative: An NWS storm survey team confirmed an EF-0 with peak winds of 85 mph touched down on the southern side of Thibodaux at 12:45am on February 15th. An trailer RV was partially flipped off of Talbot Ave as the tornado moved to the east-southeast. The tornado then reach peak strength as it impacted Tabernacle Pentecostal Church. Here, the tornado lifted a significant portion of the roof of the church, displacing it to the east. The wood framing of the roofing had evidence of rotting, so the lower bound for that damage was used in this case. The tornado slightly weakened as it moved east-southeast where minimal damage was found until it reached Percy Brown Rd where multiple large branches were snapped along it. The tornado remained very weak as it continued to the east-southeast where the next notable damage came on Crossing North St where a backyard awning was uplifted. As the tornado moved to the east-northeast, vegetation damage was noted on high-resolution imagery north of Rousseau where the tornado appeared to have lifted though additional analysis will be needed to determine the end point over inaccessible areas.

A few trees were downed here, with at least one of them taking down a powerline. The tornado tracked northeast, generally paralleling Ancil Cox Road until reaching the intersection with Old Highway 33. The most significant damage occurred near this intersection, where approximately a dozen trees were uprooted or snapped which supports the 90 mph wind rating. Beyond this point, the tornado continued northeastward producing sporadic tree and limb damage along its path. The final accessible point of the tornado���s track was near Centerville Academy. Minor damage was observed on campus, including a downed light pole, partial roof uplift on a metal building, and a baseball pitching backstop that was thrown approximately 250 feet into a chain-link fence. The tornado continued northeast beyond Lower Centreville Rd where additional minor tree damage was identified. The tornado evidently lifted over inaccessible areas to the survey team prior to reaching Hwy 48.

episode_narrative: Severe drought conditions (D2���D3) developed and intensified across portions of the New Orleans/Baton Rouge WFO area during February 2026, driven by persistent precipitation deficits and limited meaningful rainfall events. Early in the month, only isolated areas of severe drought (D2) were present across the northwestern parts of the region, but conditions steadily worsened as rainfall remained below normal, with precipitation deficits of roughly 2 to 4 inches observed across much of the region by the end of February. As a result, D2 drought expanded significantly across southern and southwestern portions of the forecast area, while pockets of extreme drought (D3) developed, particularly near coastal Louisiana. By late February, over 30 percent of the area was classified in D2 drought and more than 10 percent in D3, reflecting a rapid degradation in soil moisture and hydrologic conditions. The expansion of drought was most pronounced south of the Interstate 10 corridor, while areas farther north experienced more gradual degradation, generally remaining in D0 to D1 conditions.
event_narrative: Long term D2 to D3 drought persisted through the whole month of February for portions of Wilkinson County according to the US Drought Monitor.

episode_narrative: A band of heavy snow, coupled with gusty winds and reduced visibility, impacted east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa beginning on the afternoon of February 19, 2026, and continuing into the early morning hours of February 20, 2026. The heaviest band of snow fell generally along a line from Lincoln, NE, to Omaha, NE, to Council Bluffs, IA, with a maximum snowfall of 10.3 inches measured 4 miles southeast of Bennington, Nebraska. Numerous snowfall reports in the 7 to 9-inch range were received across Lancaster, Douglas, Sarpy, Dodge, and Saunders counties in Nebraska, as well as Pottawattamie, Mills, and Harrison counties in Iowa.||The system was forced by a broad trough moving across much of the CONUS, accompanied by a potent shortwave trough that tracked into central Nebraska. As the system took shape, a surface low maintained impressive depth, progressing slowly across northern Kansas before deepening as it pivoted and ejected from northwestern Missouri toward Wisconsin. As the low passed to the south and east, strong height falls, warm air advection, elevated instability, and frontogenesis wrapped along its northern periphery, driving a narrow but potent band of snow into east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Model soundings exhibited steep lapse rates, which supported convective snowband development and impressive snowfall rates across the area. This was coupled with wind gusts in the 25 to 35 mph range, frequently reducing visibility to below one-quarter of a mile in many locations.
event_narrative: The office received snowfall reports of 6 inches from the public, with the heaviest amounts estimated along the southern edge of the county. Measured wind gusts of 23 to 28 mph, combined with the heavy snowfall, reduced visibility to around three-quarters of a mile.

episode_narrative: A strong upper level weather system moved across the High Plains region and brought down very strong winds to the surface from the late morning to the late afternoon on February 17, 2026. A wide array of high winds in the 60 mph range affected the majority of the Texas Panhandle and some locations even experienced wind gusts over 70 mph. Damage to homes, structures, and overturned semi-trucks occurred during the afternoon as a result of these stronger winds. Blowing dust and extreme critical fire weather conditions were also present thanks to the strong winds and several wildfires occurred across the Texas Panhandle as a result.
event_narrative: The peak wind gust in Deaf Smith County was 65 mph, which was observed at the mesonet site located two miles northwest of Hereford at 1441CST. Gusts greater than 58 mph were observed in the county from about 1200CST through 1500CST.

episode_narrative: A period of extremely cold temperatures that began in late January spilled into the first week of February amid a cold airmass dominating the bulk of the country. Daytime temperatures for the start of the month struggled to rise above freezing and plummeting to sub-zero values during the overnight hours. Local cooperative observers and CoCoRaHS members recorded low temperatures ranging around minus one to minus five some mornings across southeast Ohio, with one local resident in New Lexington recording a low temperatures of minus seventeen on the morning of February 1st. While temperatures oscillated for the first week of the month in and out of freezing thresholds, strong warm air advection took hold on February 12th, which ended the cold spell. A thirty degree temperature rise was noted for daytime highs from February 9th to the 10th in response to the push of warmer temperatures filtering into the Ohio Valley.||In the midst of these very cold temperatures, a vehicle traveling on East Main Street in Pomeroy veered off the roadway, struck a utility pole, and plunged into the icy Ohio River in Meigs County. The driver was pronounced dead at the scene, but her body was not immediately recovered until the middle of March down river in Greenup County, Kentucky. A young juvenile occupant inside the car was rescued by first responders and transported to a hospital on the evening of the crash with minor injuries.

episode_narrative: Lack of rainfall, top five-ten heat, and a flash drought situation with extremely low top-soil moisture levels allowed Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to worsen as February approached March.  Exceptional (D4) Drought developed on the 17th across the Brush Country - just the fourth small area in the nation at the time (others were in the Texas Big Bend, central Colorado, and northeast Arkansas).  By month's end, the Texas Agrilife Crop and Weather report described soil moisture conditions as extremely poor, with range and pasture forages in poor condition and in some cases, cattle ranchers were liquidating herds. ||Loss/impact reports will be provided for the end of March StormData, when region-wide seasonal drought conditions peaked.
event_narrative: Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions arrived in west-central Brooks County on the 17th, continuing through the end of the month, while Extreme (D3) conditions prevailed across all but the southeast sliver, before they, too, moved to D3 on the 24th. The introduction of D4, for the first time in five years for the Brush Country/Rio Grande Plains, was due to the combination of prolonged rain-free conditions, along with heat and low to very low humidity on many days.

episode_narrative: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

episode_narrative: Robust bands of snow tracked through the state of West Virginia from February 6th to the 7th, leading to snow amounts ranging from 3 to 6 inches along the mountains and 1 to 3 inches in the lower elevations. A frontal passage that occurred during this event also led to a brief stint of strong surface wind gusts ranging from 35 to 52 miles per hour. Behind the front, additional snow squalls and dangerous cold filtered into the Central Appalachians. High pressure shifting in from the west allowed for snow showers to taper off quickly after sunrise on February 7th.

episode_narrative: The severe to extreme drought conditions that became entrenched across central Indiana during the winter of 2025-2026 persisted through the month of February. While January had seen a significant degradation and expansion of drought intensity, February was characterized by a stagnant status quo, where meager precipitation totals prevented any meaningful recovery. Extreme Drought (D3) remained fixed across the north-central corridor, while Severe Drought (D2) continued to blanket much of the surrounding West Central and Central Indiana counties.||The most intense conditions remained centered on Howard County, which stayed entirely within D3 intensity throughout the month. This Extreme Drought also maintained its grip on much of Carroll and Delaware counties, the northern half of Tipton County, and the northern third of Madison County. Furthermore, D3 conditions remained fixed in the far northwestern corner of Randolph County and northeastern Clinton County. Surrounding these areas, D2 conditions were maintained across the entirety of Warren, Tippecanoe, Fountain, and Vermillion counties, as well as the majority of Boone, Hamilton, and Montgomery counties. On the southern fringe of the drought���s extent, D2 intensity persisted in northwestern Parke, northwestern Vigo, and northern Henry counties.||Precipitation throughout February was once again critically low, frequently falling well below 50% of monthly norms. The driest conditions were observed in the northwest, where Warren County recorded less than a tenth of an inch of liquid equivalent, and Tippecanoe County saw only around 0.20 inches. Other hard-hit areas, including Carroll, Howard, and Delaware counties, saw totals struggle to reach 1.00 inch. While southern and eastern fringes like Henry and Parke counties received slightly higher totals ranging from 1.50 to 2.00 inches, the moisture was insufficient to overcome the long-term deficits. While D2 conditions were proscribed to end in March for several counties���including Vigo, Hamilton, and Boone���the drought remained firmly established for the majority of the region as the month concluded.
event_narrative: Precipitation totaled only around 1.10 inches across the month of February. This maintained D2 conditions across portions of Randolph county with D3 conditions in the far northwest. These drought conditions continued into at least March 2026.

episode_narrative: On the third of February, a tornado formed in Plum Grove area in Liberty county.
event_narrative: Storms moved through Liberty county on February 3rd, where a tornado warned storm passed through the Plum Grove area. Initially broadcast media reported trees down near intersection of County Road 3709 and County Road 3732. In the aftermath of this storm, a survey team was dispatched to assess the damage across the area.||The survey team found that this storm produced two tornadoes, this being the first. According to the survey team, the tornado appeared to initially touched down within a wooded area between CR 3708 and CR 3709, then turned eastward along CR 3709 for a short distance before lifting up shortly before River Ln. A drone was used to assess an areal view of the damage, though the survey team noted that they did not see any damage in the deeply wooded area along the East Fork of the San Jacinto River. Therefore, the survey team concluded that the first tornado ended just before the River Ln and CR 3709 intersection. The majority of the damage seen was broken trunks and branches of pine trees and fences down. Power lines were also reported blown down, but the power line poles remained upright. This tornado was rated as an EF0 with a maximum estimated wind speed of 80 mph. This maximum wind speed was based on Softwood Trees (TS) with a DOD of 2. Survey teams noted that the trees in question had reported beetle damage.

episode_narrative: Above normal temperatures and below normal precipitation continued through the month of February. This led to a continued state of drought across eastern Utah and western Colorado, particularly along the northern and central Colorado Divide mountains. Extreme (D3) Drought saw expansion during the middle of the month, moving into portions of lower elevation northwest Colorado.
event_narrative: At the beginning of the month of February, the US Drought Monitor analyzed an area of Exceptional (D4) Drought as covering roughly 35% of Colorado Zone 010 - Gore and Elk Mountains/Central Mountain Valleys. Exceptional (D3) Drought covered 45% of the zone, with Severe (D2) covering 19%, and Moderate (D1) covering 1%. With the 2/11 US Drought Monitor update, Exceptional (D4) Drought remained unchanged, at 35% coverage. Extreme (D3) Drought expanded to 50% coverage, with Severe (D2) Drought shrinking to 15% coverage, and Moderate (D1) Drought being removed. From this point through the end of the month, drought conditions remained unchanged in the zone. No reports of damages or impacts from drought conditions have been received.

episode_narrative: In the days leading up to this event, a strong trough made landfall along the West Coast of the US. Ahead of this system, unusually warm and dry conditions prevailed as high pressure dominated the Intermountain West. The trough began to track inland on the 15th into the 16th, but the high pressure was reluctant to shift east. This led to a tightening up of the pressure gradient between these two features, enhancing an already strong southwesterly upper level jet. Lift began to increase ahead of the trough on the evening of the 16th, with mountain rain and snow showers breaking out over the higher terrain of eastern Utah and western Colorado. This also helped to keep deep mixing ongoing well after sunset, resulting in some of the peak winds occurring between midnight and daybreak on the 17th. In addition, a potent cold front was associated with this system, and was expected to sweep through eastern Utah and western Colorado around daybreak. Ahead of the cold front, the surface pressure gradient tightened substantially and surface winds maxed out. This coincided with the period between midnight and daybreak on the 17th.
event_narrative: The peak gust of 72 mph was recorded at the Utah Department of Transportation mesonet site I-70 at MP 226 Harley Dome at 3:10 AM MST 2/17. The peak gust to be recorded at an ASOS or AWOS was 69 mph at KCNY ASOS at Canyonlands Airport, north of Moab, UT. Two gusts to 69 mph were recorded at KCNY, one at 2:32 AM MST 2/17, and one at 2:33 AM MST 2/17. Additional gusts at various sensors across the zone ranged from 45 mph to 58 mph during the period of highest winds. No reports of damages, injuries, or fatalities associated with this high wind event have been received.

episode_narrative: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.
event_narrative: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Stewart County remained under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions throughout February. Following the initial onset of D2 on October 28, 2025, the county experienced a brief period of mid-winter marginal improvement before conditions degraded back to D2 levels in January. By the end of February, the county had recorded a total of 14 weeks at or above the D2 threshold, with drought conditions persisting into March.

A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.
event_narrative: The Tygart Valley River at Mill Creek rose above a bankfull level of 11 feet on the afternoon of February 20th, then continued to rise to a crest around 13 feet later that afternoon. A slowly sinking cold front provided lift for thunderstorm development during the evening hours across north Mississippi. Partial clearing of skies prior to the frontal arrival resulted in moderate destabilization. Climatologically, February is cooler, which increases confidence in very cold air aloft. The lift from the front, an unstable environment, and cold air aloft raised a primary concern for large hail. Elevated MUCAPE values (up to 1500 J/kg) and steep lapse rates resulted in hail up to golf ball size to occur.

episode_narrative: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across the Ozarks but limited precipitation through the month allowed Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to develop across portions of far south central Missouri. Some expansion of drought conditions occurred through the month across portions of southwestern Missouri as well. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
event_narrative: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced continued dry conditions with drought remaining Severe (D2) drought to Moderate (D1) drought in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

episode_narrative: A storm force low moved into the Bering on February 8. Once the front pushed onshore by February 10, blizzard conditions were observed in the Kuskokwim Delta Coast for a time. Once the low approached the mainland, another period of blizzard conditions were observed in the Kuskokwim Delta on February 12.

episode_narrative: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of McCurtain County Oklahoma through the month of February. Rainfall amounts during February only tallied to 1.50-2.50 inches,  which was only half or less the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, extreme (D3) drought had expanded across the southern half of McCurtain County during the final few weeks of the month.

A drier than normal winter concluded with one of the driest Februarys on record across central and southeast Illinois. In Lincoln, only 0.08 inches of rainfall occurred during the month. Dating back to September 2025, precipitation deficits of 6 to 10 inches were common across the region. Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought conditions worsened during February 2026, with a notable uptick in reported impacts and community restrictions (such as water rationing and burn bans). Streamflows, water levels, and soil moisture content ranged from well below normal to near record lows.
event_narrative: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to the Fall of 2025, Severe Drought (D2) was ongoing at the start of the month. Lincoln experienced their driest February on record, with the official observation recording just 0.08 of precipitation, which was 1.84 inches below normal. Dating back to last September, the precipitation deficit for Lincoln was more than 7 inches. Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought was in place across the county by the end of the month.

episode_narrative: A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Most of these tornadoes were brief, and none were stronger than EF-1, but one serious injury occurred in Crawford County as a result of a tornado. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.

episode_narrative: A strengthening storm system lifted through the Middle Mississippi Valley on the 19th, dragging its warm frontal zone northward through the Midwest, and bringing near-record high temperatures and anomalous dewpoints into central Indiana.  Multiple rounds of severe weather occurred over the region, from early morning large hail in two far-northern zones, covering roads in Warren County, to more organized evening severe weather from rotating supercell thunderstorms.  Through the evening of the 19th, the destabilized atmosphere combined with a stregthening low-level jet stream that progressed eastward into the region, boosting 0-1 km wind shear as high as 300 m2/s2.  A resultant cluster of discrete late-day to evening supercells were focused along the frontal zone, near or south of the Interstate 70 corridor, and produced scattered large hail over 6 counties and isolated wind damage to trees and/or power poles in 4 counties.  ||A stronger supercell with a history of producing two weak tornadoes in Crawford County, Illinois, continued into central Indiana, spawning an EF-0 tornado in Sullivan County, an intense EF-2 just west of Bloomington that caused extensive structural damage to homes, apartments, and airport facilities, and a brief EF-U in Decatur County;  this cell also produced ping-pong ball (1.50-inch diameter) sized hail in Greene and Monroe Counties.

episode_narrative: A prolonged period of wintry weather impacted eastern Kentucky from February 22 into February 24, 2026, as a deep upper-level trough over the eastern United States funneled a moist, modified polar airmass into the region. This setup established a persistent northwesterly upslope flow regime, resulting in scattered to numerous snow showers. These showers were frequently cellular in nature and produced squall-like conditions at some locations.||Accumulations varied significantly across the region due to the convective and orographic nature of the event. While many locations near and west of Pottsville Escarpment saw only a dusting to an inch, higher terrain in the southeast experienced much more substantial totals. The heaviest totals were generally concentrated near the Pine and Black Mountains in the far east, where persistent upslope forcing maximized snowfall. However, isolated similarly heavy swaths were also noted upstream of these higher mountains over portions of Lee and Owsley counties, where convective snow bands persisted for extended periods. Despite high snow-to-liquid ratios of 15:1 to 40:1 for most locations, leading to dry, fluffy snow, the intensity of the showers caused slick and hazardous travel conditions on untreated roads.
event_narrative: An isolated, heavy swath of snow developed upstream of the main eastern Kentucky mountain ranges. A trained spotter and retired NWS employee at Belle Point measured a storm total of 6.5 inches of snow by 0930EST on the 23rd. A CO-OP observer 4 miles north of Beattyville recorded 2.6 inches during the same event.

episode_narrative: A winter storm system tracked across the West Coast, North Slope, and Interior Alaska from February 20 through February 25, 2026. The episode began with widespread blizzard conditions impacting the West Coast and North Slope regions, where powerful winds and significant blowing snow reduced visibilities to near zero. As the system pushed inland, it transitioned into a heavy snow event for the Central and Eastern Interior. Notable snowfall reports included thirteen and one-half inches measured northwest of Ester and nearly nine inches reported by storm spotters in the Tanana Valley. Additionally, measurements from the Nenana Snotel indicated a seven-inch snow depth increase over a twenty-four-hour period during the height of the storm. These conditions created hazardous travel and significant impacts to infrastructure across the state. No fatalities or injuries were reported during this episode.
event_narrative: A heavy snow event impacted the Goldstream Valley and Nenana Hills, where a winter storm warning was in effect from 1027AKST on February 21 through 1159AKST on February 24, 2026. The Keystone Ridge Cooperative Observer site (KERA2) recorded an increase in snow depth from thirty-three inches at 1200AKST on February 21 to thirty-five inches at 1200AKST on February 22, then reaching forty-one inches at 1200AKST on February 23. A public report northwest of Ester confirmed thirteen and one-half inches of snow accumulation. The peak of the event occurred at 1716AKST on February 22 at the Fairbanks International Airport (PAFA), where the station reported three-quarters of a mile visibility in light snow and mist. The first verifying observation for the heavy snow occurred at 1155AKST on February 24. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

event_narrative: The Ranger Road fire was a large wildfire that began in Beaver County, OK during the early afternoon hours of February 17th. Fueled by strong southwesterly winds and low relative humidity, the fire spread quickly into Kansas. Evacuations were ordered for the town of Englewood, Ashland, and all of southern Clark County. Two firefighters were injured battling the blaze in the county. It was reported by local ranchers that hundreds of cattle perished in the fire. The exact acreage burned in Clark County is unknown, but the total acreage burned from the fire was 283,383. The fire was controlled February 24.

episode_narrative: Strong mid-upper level trough ejected into the Plains early on February 17 which led to a rapid deepening of a surface cyclone. Strong winds developed behind the cold frontal passage, leading to numerous high wind reports across central and western Kansas. Large wildfires spread quickly as a result of the strong winds.
event_narrative: Kansas Forest Service reported the Andrew Lane fire began in Seward County before spreading into nearby Meade County. The exact acreage in Seward County is unknown, but the fire burned a total of 7,217 acres. The fire began on February 17, and was controlled by February 20. episode_narrative: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
event_narrative: Tin roofing material removed from a fishing camp. Time estimated by radar.

episode_narrative: Severe drought conditions (D2���D3) developed and intensified across portions of the New Orleans/Baton Rouge WFO area during February 2026, driven by persistent precipitation deficits and limited meaningful rainfall events. Early in the month, only isolated areas of severe drought (D2) were present across the northwestern parts of the region, but conditions steadily worsened as rainfall remained below normal, with precipitation deficits of roughly 2 to 4 inches observed across much of the region by the end of February. As a result, D2 drought expanded significantly across southern and southwestern portions of the forecast area, while pockets of extreme drought (D3) developed, particularly near coastal Louisiana. By late February, over 30 percent of the area was classified in D2 drought and more than 10 percent in D3, reflecting a rapid degradation in soil moisture and hydrologic conditions. The expansion of drought was most pronounced south of the Interstate 10 corridor, while areas farther north experienced more gradual degradation, generally remaining in D0 to D1 conditions.
event_narrative: Prolonged D2 to D3 drought effected portions of West Feliciana Parish for the entire month of February.

episode_narrative: A band of heavy snow, coupled with gusty winds and reduced visibility, impacted east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa beginning on the afternoon of February 19, 2026, and continuing into the early morning hours of February 20, 2026. The heaviest band of snow fell generally along a line from Lincoln, NE, to Omaha, NE, to Council Bluffs, IA, with a maximum snowfall of 10.3 inches measured 4 miles southeast of Bennington, Nebraska. Numerous snowfall reports in the 7 to 9-inch range were received across Lancaster, Douglas, Sarpy, Dodge, and Saunders counties in Nebraska, as well as Pottawattamie, Mills, and Harrison counties in Iowa.||The system was forced by a broad trough moving across much of the CONUS, accompanied by a potent shortwave trough that tracked into central Nebraska. As the system took shape, a surface low maintained impressive depth, progressing slowly across northern Kansas before deepening as it pivoted and ejected from northwestern Missouri toward Wisconsin. As the low passed to the south and east, strong height falls, warm air advection, elevated instability, and frontogenesis wrapped along its northern periphery, driving a narrow but potent band of snow into east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Model soundings exhibited steep lapse rates, which supported convective snowband development and impressive snowfall rates across the area. This was coupled with wind gusts in the 25 to 35 mph range, frequently reducing visibility to below one-quarter of a mile in many locations.
event_narrative: The office received snowfall reports of 5 inches from the public, with the heaviest amounts of 6-7 inches estimated along the eastern edge of the county. Measured wind gusts of 20 to 27 mph, combined with the heavy snowfall, reduced visibility to around one-half mile.

episode_narrative: A low pressure system tracking through the Great Lakes lifted a series of fronts through eastern New York, resulting in widespread precipitation from Friday, February 20 through Saturday, February 21, 2026. Elsewhere, a couple of tenths up to 5 inches were common with the highest of these reported across the Catskills, Helderbergs, and Taconics. Fortunately, freezing rain accumulations were more apparent based on radar products rather than in ground-truth observations so little in the way of impacts occurred due to ice accretion. ||Key impacts: school delays and traffic accidents.

episode_narrative: A period of extremely cold temperatures that began in late January spilled into the first week of February amid a cold airmass dominating the bulk of the country. Daytime temperatures for the start of the month struggled to rise above freezing and plummeting to sub-zero values during the overnight hours. Local cooperative observers and CoCoRaHS members recorded low temperatures ranging around minus one to minus five some mornings across southeast Ohio, with one local resident in New Lexington recording a low temperatures of minus seventeen on the morning of February 1st. While temperatures oscillated for the first week of the month in and out of freezing thresholds, strong warm air advection took hold on February 12th, which ended the cold spell. A thirty degree temperature rise was noted for daytime highs from February 9th to the 10th in response to the push of warmer temperatures filtering into the Ohio Valley.||In the midst of these very cold temperatures, a vehicle traveling on East Main Street in Pomeroy veered off the roadway, struck a utility pole, and plunged into the icy Ohio River in Meigs County. The driver was pronounced dead at the scene, but her body was not immediately recovered until the middle of March down river in Greenup County, Kentucky. A young juvenile occupant inside the car was rescued by first responders and transported to a hospital on the evening of the crash with minor injuries.

episode_narrative: Dry conditions occurred across the Oklahoma Panhandle to start February. A cold front dropped south through the region on February 10th and brought breezy winds and at least elevated fire weather conditions to the region. This resulted in the development of two wildfires in Beaver County, Oklahoma.
event_narrative: The Flat Tire wildfire ignited at approximately 11:35 a.m. on February 10, 2026, in Beaver County, Oklahoma. The fire was located south of the town of Turpin, or 1/4 of a mile east of the intersection NS123 and EW10. It burned in and around the Beaver River bottom area. This fire was human caused. Officials noted that a flat tire had blown off and sparked, which caused the ignition. The fire was fueled by exceptional fuel loading in the county. The fire burned 1,983 acres. No damage to homes or major structures occurred with this fire. However, US Highway 83 was closed on February 10th in Turpin to US Highway 412 due to the fire.

Widespread totals in excess of 6 inches were noted across much of northeast Iowa.
event_narrative: This snow band brought heavy snow to Allamakee County with snowfall totals ranging from 8 to 13 inches. The highest reported snowfall total in the county was in Waukon where 13 inches was measured.

episode_narrative: A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

event_narrative: At the beginning of the month of February, the US Drought Monitor analyzed an area of Extreme (D3) Drought covering roughly 10% of Colorado Zone 013 - Flattop Mountains. Severe (D2) Drought covered 80% of the zone, with Moderate (D1) Drought covering the remaining 10%. With the 2/4 Drought Monitor update, Extreme (D3) Drought expanded to cover roughly 75% of the zone, with the remaining 25% under Severe (D2) Drought. Between this point and the end of the month, there were no changes to drought conditions in this zone. No reports of impacts or damages related to this drought were received.

episode_narrative: Winds on the 18th were generally weaker than the winds that had occurred with cold-frontal passage the day before. However, a strong northwesterly jet remained aloft, and daytime mixing allowed for stronger, post-frontal winds to gust across the region. Particularly, northwest to southeast oriented valleys, and areas around the Four Corners, are favored under this type of post-frontal regime.
event_narrative: The peak, and only, gust to be recorded during this event in this zone was 58 mph at KMTJ ASOS at Montrose Regional Airport in Montrose, CO. The gust occurred at 10:11 AM MST. No other gusts above 45 mph were recorded on this day, though that does not discount that gusts to this level or above occurred, as there are only so many sensors in the zone. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities associated with this high wind event were received.

episode_narrative: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.
event_narrative: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Bibb County remained under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions throughout February. Following the initial onset of D2 on November 25, 2025, the county experienced a brief period of marginal improvement before conditions degraded back to D2 levels in January. By the end of February, the county had recorded a total of ten weeks at or above the D2 threshold, with drought conditions persisting into March.

On February 23rd, strong Nor'easter system moved northeast in the Atlantic, east of Cape Cod. It moved northeast through the Gulf of Maine, just south of Nova Scotia. Strong winds and plenty of moisture resulted in blizzard conditions in coastal Hancock, and central and coastal Washington county. Blizzard conditions verified during the afternoon of the 23rd in these areas. Heavy snow fell during the morning into the evening of the 23rd for northern Hancock county, with totals roughly 4 - 8 inches. Bangor region roughly got 1 - 5 inches of snow. Central Highlands, Upper Penobscot Valley, southern and eastern Aroostook county had accumulations around 1-2 inches. North Woods region only accumulated about a trace - 1 inch of snow. High winds results in isolated power outages, predominantly in Hancock county. Multiple school closures in Downeast region. Low pressure moved east of Maine by nighttime, with precipitation gradually slowing down.
event_narrative: Storm total snow accumulations ranged from 1 to 4 inches.

A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.

episode_narrative: Low pressure system from the west moved over Maine, late on 02/10 into 02/11. Occluded front moves over the state, bringing precipitation in the form of snow from west to southeast. Low began to slow down over eastern Maine, and alongside a surface low developing, heaviest snowfall occurred over eastern Maine.
