episode_narrative: A highly anticipated, highly impactful Nor'easter struck northwest Connecticut on the evening of Sunday, February 22 through the afternoon of Monday, February 23, 2026. Tracking along the East Coast and rapidly intensifying as it approached the 40 latitude/70 longitude benchmark, this system quickly gained national attention not only for its projected widespread blizzard conditions across many high profile, highly populated areas, but for the complexity of its forecast. ||Confidence increased sufficiently for forecasters at National Weather Service Albany to upgrade a prior issued Winter Storm Warning to a Blizzard Warning mere hours prior to snowfall onset in Litchfield County. Once snow began, it didn't take long for rates to become moderate to heavy, rapidly dropping visibility late in the evening of Sunday, February 22nd. As the core of the still strengthening storm drew closer, winds became gusty and reduced visibility further. The combination of heavy snowfall rates and frequent wind gusts between 25 to 40 mph made for on and off blizzard conditions, with visibilities falling below one quarter of a mile, from around 2 AM through nearly 1230 PM Monday, February 23, 2026. Snow finally began to gradually slow after 1230 PM Monday, February 23, 2026 and eventually tapered off after 4 PM. The resulting snowfall totals across Litchfield County reached 12 to nearly 20 inches. ||Ahead of the event, the Governor of Connecticut, Ned Lamont, declared a State of Emergency in an attempt to keep residents off the roads. Consequently, many schools; local businesses; and roadways were closed, and there was a travel ban instated for commercial vehicles beginning at 5 PM on Sunday, February 22nd. Additionally, and unfortunately, there was one recorded death in New Milford in southern Litchfield County. The age and sex of the individual were not available, nor was the location in which they died. However, per the medical examiner's office, the individual died of 'accidental hypothermia' that was likely exacerbated by their prior ailments of dementia and cardiovascular disease. ||Key Impacts: state of emergency, travel ban, road closures, traffic accidents, school closures, power outages.
event_narrative: Zone average snowfall of 15 inches and 3 to 4 hours worth of frequent wind gusts between 35 to 40 mph.

episode_narrative: A winter storm impacted much of southeast South Carolina with significant snow accumulations on January 31st along with very cold wind chill temperatures persisting into late morning February 1st. An area of low pressure shifted off the Southeast Coast while deepening, ushering in a very cold air mass across the region. Snow accumulation ended by midnight on January 31st, but hazardous traveling conditions and very cold wind chill temperatures persisted through morning hours on February 1st.

episode_narrative: Throughout February 2026, drought conditions in Maine remained stable in their classification from the USDM, maintaining extreme to severe drought conditions. By the end of the month, Maine���s drought coverage was nearly 1% Extreme Drought (D3), 53% Severe Drought (D2), and 46% Moderate Drought (D1). The freeze cap locked down any recharge to the system groundwater, while surface hydrologic conditions showed signs of continued deterioration with below normal precipitation. Precipitation during February was notably insufficient, with much of the region recording less than 50% of normal accumulations. This deficit was compounded by deep soil frost depths ranging from 6 to 20 inches, which acted as an impermeable barrier and prevented any melting snow or rain from recharging stressed aquifers. Consequently, groundwater levels in southern Maine continued to decline, reaching or falling below the historic lows observed during the 2002 drought. While snow was present across the state, the snowpack remained below normal in central and northern regions, and hundreds of households reported dry private wells due to the persistent lack of recovery.
event_narrative: Franklin County averaged 1.68 inches of precipitation in February, approximately 2.02 inches below normal, making it the 3rd driest February. The USDM on February 24th had 85% of the county in Severe Drought (D2) and 15% in Extreme Drought (D3).

episode_narrative: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

episode_narrative: Eastern Oklahoma experienced only one rainfall event during the month of February. During this mid-month event, rainfall across the region ranged from one hundredth to one tenth of an inch across portions of northeastern Oklahoma to as much as three to four inches across portions of east central and southeastern Oklahoma. The rainfall that fell across eastern Oklahoma in February was below the monthly average amounts for much of the region, with a large portion of northeastern Oklahoma only receiving from one to five percent of monthly average precipitation amounts. These very dry conditions, compounding on several months of dry weather, allowed the drought that developed across portions of the region in January to expand in February. Severe (D2) drought conditions developed across all of Washington, Nowata, Craig, Ottawa, Rogers, Mayes, Delaware, Wagoner, and Cherokee Counties, and developed across portions of Tulsa, Muskogee, Adair, McIntosh, Pittsburg, Pushmataha, and Choctaw Counties. Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed into portions of Choctaw, Ottawa, Delaware, Mayes, Wagoner, Cherokee, Muskogee and Adair Counties during the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

episode_narrative: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.

Following the initial onset of D2 on November 18, 2025, the county sustained 15 consecutive weeks of D2 conditions as of the end of February. These conditions persisted into March.

episode_narrative: Drought conditions developed in the Ozark Foothills of Southeast Missouri early September due to a very dry August and first half of September. While conditions improved with October rainfall, D2 (Severe Drought) remained in northwestern Carter County and southwestern Ripley County through the end of year and expanded through Wayne and Butler Counties during January. Very dry conditions continued through February with a half inch to an inch of precipitation for the month, around 2.5-3 below normal, and the 2nd driest February in Poplar Bluff. The entirety of winter across Southeast Missouri finished with record low winter precipitation, with 2.44 at Poplar Bluff. By the end of February, roughly half of Carter and Ripley Counties had changed to D3 (Extreme Drought) status. Occurring in between the '25 and '26 growing seasons, impacts from drought in February were very limited. Drought conditions continued into March.

A potent area of low pressure stationed across southern Ontario allowed for a surface cold front to begin tracking across the Great Lake region during that afternoon and evening hours of February 6, 2026. As this cold front approached portions of central Pennsylvania, rapid drops in visibility were beginning to be observed on webcams due to snow squalls. These snow squalls continued across portions of southwestern Pennsylvania during the late evening hours of February 6th, mainly across Somerset County. As the cold front continued progressing across the region, snow showers intensity waned; however, an isolated snow squall in Schuylkill County was also observed with a rapid drop to near-zero visibility on Interstate 81. Cold air and gusty winds in the wake of the cold frontal passage allowed for dangerously cold wind chills across much of western Pennsylvania. No injuries or fatalities were reported with these snow squalls and the extreme cold that followed the cold frontal passage as temperatures began to warm during the late morning and early afternoon hours of February 7th.

After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.

episode_narrative: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across the Ozarks but limited precipitation through the month allowed Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to develop across portions of far south central Missouri. Some expansion of drought conditions occurred through the month across portions of southwestern Missouri as well. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
event_narrative: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced continued dry conditions with drought remaining Severe (D2) drought to Moderate (D1) drought in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

episode_narrative: A drier than normal winter concluded with one of the driest Februarys on record across central and southeast Illinois. In Lincoln, only 0.08 inches of rainfall occurred during the month. Dating back to September 2025, precipitation deficits of 6 to 10 inches were common across the region. Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought conditions worsened during February 2026, with a notable uptick in reported impacts and community restrictions (such as water rationing and burn bans). Streamflows, water levels, and soil moisture content ranged from well below normal to near record lows.
event_narrative: Drought conditions worsened and became Severe (D2) during the month. Streamflows and soil moisture values across the region ranged from well below normal to near record lows, and there were reports that dry wells necessitated water hauling.

episode_narrative: A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Most of these tornadoes were brief, and none were stronger than EF-1, but one serious injury occurred in Crawford County as a result of a tornado. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.

An upper level trough ejected east-northeast from the Desert Southwest into Northwest Texas and Western Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of February 14th, which resulted in the increase of very warm, humid air north across the region from the Gulf. In advance of this system, southwest flow aloft became established, with increasing instability at the surface and aloft coupled with strong wind shear and an approaching cold front enhancing large scale ascent across much of the Four State Region. As a result, showers and thunderstorms, some of which became severe over portions of East Texas and Central Louisiana, developed and spread east across the area during the late afternoon through the evening. Multiple reports of wind damage were received, with a brief, weak isolated tornado having been spawned in Northeast Shelby County near the James community.
event_narrative: This brief EF-1 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 95 mph began along County Road 3156, where a few trees were downed, and then it traveled southeast to cross Highway 7 where it intersected with County Road 3153. Most of the damage here was also to trees with a consolidated area of snapped softwood trees giving the tornado its estimated maximum windspeed rating. The tornado then continued to the southeast and was judged to have ended just after crossing County Road 3215. One outbuilding was destroyed at this location, but otherwise the survey team could verify only minor damage done to a few buildings here and earlier when the tornado crossed Highway 7. Localized snapping of tree trunks was also quite evident around a pond just to the west of County Road 3215.

episode_narrative: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and development of extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across portions of Southwest Arkansas through the month of February. Rainfall amounts during February only tallied to 0.50-2.00+ inches, which was less than half of the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, extreme (D3) drought developed across Northern Howard County Arkansas by the second week of the month.

A strengthening storm system lifted through the Middle Mississippi Valley on the 19th, dragging its warm frontal zone northward through the Midwest, and bringing near-record high temperatures and anomalous dewpoints into central Indiana.  Multiple rounds of severe weather occurred over the region, from early morning large hail in two far-northern zones, covering roads in Warren County, to more organized evening severe weather from rotating supercell thunderstorms.  Through the evening of the 19th, the destabilized atmosphere combined with a stregthening low-level jet stream that progressed eastward into the region, boosting 0-1 km wind shear as high as 300 m2/s2.  A resultant cluster of discrete late-day to evening supercells were focused along the frontal zone, near or south of the Interstate 70 corridor, and produced scattered large hail over 6 counties and isolated wind damage to trees and/or power poles in 4 counties.  ||A stronger supercell with a history of producing two weak tornadoes in Crawford County, Illinois, continued into central Indiana, spawning an EF-0 tornado in Sullivan County, an intense EF-2 just west of Bloomington that caused extensive structural damage to homes, apartments, and airport facilities, and a brief EF-U in Decatur County;  this cell also produced ping-pong ball (1.50-inch diameter) sized hail in Greene and Monroe Counties.
event_narrative: An EF-0 tornado tracked 4.10 miles over southern Sullivan County, between the Paxton and Carlisle communities. The maximum path width was 300 yards with multiple outbuildings significantly or completely destroyed and damage to trees.  The supercell originally spawned two weak tornadoes in Crawford County, Illinois, which lifted before crossing the Wabash River into southwestern Sullivan County near Indiana Route 58. The tornado appeared to frequently come in contact with the ground at a few locations east of Route 58 but never remained in contact with the ground for a long distance, yet demonstrated damage that reflects high-end EF0 winds around 80 mph. The tornado maintained EF-0 intensity as it moved east-northeast through agricultural land, snapping a mix of large hardwood and softwood trees before lifting from Sullivan County. Damage was observed just northwest of Carlisle, where several small outbuildings sustained major damage. In this location, wind speeds were estimated at 80 mph, consistent with EF-0 intensity. The tornado continued across US-41 just south of Paxton, where the strongest damage, an additional outbuilding completely destroyed along with several large trees knocked over and snapped, was consistent with winds upwards of 85 mph;  the storm survey estimates that the width of the tree damage spanned around 300 yards in an adjacent field.  Peak wind speeds were estimated at 85 mph.

episode_narrative: A winter storm system tracked across the West Coast, North Slope, and Interior Alaska from February 20 through February 25, 2026. The episode began with widespread blizzard conditions impacting the West Coast and North Slope regions, where powerful winds and significant blowing snow reduced visibilities to near zero. As the system pushed inland, it transitioned into a heavy snow event for the Central and Eastern Interior. Notable snowfall reports included thirteen and one-half inches measured northwest of Ester and nearly nine inches reported by storm spotters in the Tanana Valley. Additionally, measurements from the Nenana Snotel indicated a seven-inch snow depth increase over a twenty-four-hour period during the height of the storm. These conditions created hazardous travel and significant impacts to infrastructure across the state. No fatalities or injuries were reported during this episode.
event_narrative: Blizzard conditions impacted Kivalina, where a Blizzard Warning was in effect from 0431AKST February 20 until 0843AKST February 22, 2026. The Kivalina Airport AWOS (PAVL) initially reported blizzard conditions at 2300AKST February 20, with blizzard conditions continuing through 0415AKST February 22. At 0046AKST February 21, PAVL reported one-quarter of a mile visibility in freezing fog with sustained winds of thirty-five miles per hour and a peak gust of fifty-six miles per hour. The Blizzard Warning verified at 0200AKST February 21, when PAVL reported a third hour of blizzard conditions with visibility less than one-quarter of a mile in freezing fog with sustained winds of thirty-seven miles per hour gusting to forty-eight miles per hour. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

episode_narrative: A strong Bering Sea low moves into the Gulf of Anadyr, allowing for a strong front to move into Western Alaska. As the front approached the West Coast, strong east/southeast winds brought blizzard and whiteout conditions to much of the Seward Peninsula south. A secondary push of moisture brought by a shortwave system pushed off the Bering Sea low allowed for widespread heavy snow across St. Lawrence Island, the southern Seward Peninsula, and parts of the Western Interior. As the front pushed eastward across the state, snow squalls developed over portions of the Central Interior, leading to periods of heavy snowfall and gusty winds.

episode_narrative: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
event_narrative: An NWS Storm Survey team determined that an EF-1 tornado with peak winds of 105 mph embedded in a line of storms touched down just north of the Ascension/Assumption Parish line shortly after midnight on February 15th. This tornado started by snapping large branches and uprooting a tree on Te Nom Landry Rd and Highway 308 south. It continued moving east-northeast over open fields until reaching the intersection of Highway 3089 and Highway 70. Here, the tornado strengthened to EF-1 intensity where a power pole and tree trunk were snapped. This tornado maintained intensity as it continued moving to the east-northeast where it snapped a series of powerlines off of Baxter Rd on the south side of the CF Industries complex. The tornado then started to intensify to peak intensity as it crossed into St. James Parish while moving through mainly open fields before it hit a series of powerlines in an open field, snapping 4 lines. It maintained strength as it crossed another open field along Badger Rd before snapping another series of powerlines along Highway 18. The tornado appeared to weaken as it continued to move east-northeast across the Mississippi River. When the tornado reached Highway 3125, it partially snapped/bent another powerline. The tornado then moved into the marsh north of Highway 3025 before reaching Highway 61 where it uprooted another tree. The last damage point for this tornado is along I-10 where it snapped more large branches.

A band of heavy snow, coupled with gusty winds and reduced visibility, impacted east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa beginning on the afternoon of February 19, 2026, and continuing into the early morning hours of February 20, 2026. The heaviest band of snow fell generally along a line from Lincoln, NE, to Omaha, NE, to Council Bluffs, IA, with a maximum snowfall of 10.3 inches measured 4 miles southeast of Bennington, Nebraska. Numerous snowfall reports in the 7 to 9-inch range were received across Lancaster, Douglas, Sarpy, Dodge, and Saunders counties in Nebraska, as well as Pottawattamie, Mills, and Harrison counties in Iowa.||The system was forced by a broad trough moving across much of the CONUS, accompanied by a potent shortwave trough that tracked into central Nebraska. As the system took shape, a surface low maintained impressive depth, progressing slowly across northern Kansas before deepening as it pivoted and ejected from northwestern Missouri toward Wisconsin. As the low passed to the south and east, strong height falls, warm air advection, elevated instability, and frontogenesis wrapped along its northern periphery, driving a narrow but potent band of snow into east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Model soundings exhibited steep lapse rates, which supported convective snowband development and impressive snowfall rates across the area. This was coupled with wind gusts in the 25 to 35 mph range, frequently reducing visibility to below one-quarter of a mile in many locations.

episode_narrative: A highly anticipated, highly impactful Nor'easter struck eastern New York on the evening of Sunday, February 22 through the afternoon of Monday, February 23, 2026. Tracking along the East Coast and rapidly intensifying as it approached the 40 latitude/70 longitude benchmark, this system quickly gained national attention not only for its projected widespread blizzard conditions across many high profile, highly populated areas, but for the complexity of its forecast.||Confidence increased sufficiently for forecasters at National Weather Service Albany to upgrade prior issued Winter Storm Warnings to a Blizzard Warnings in Dutchess and Ulster Counties mere hours prior to snowfall onset. Once snow began, it didn't take long for rates to become moderate to heavy, particularly across Dutchess and eastern Ulster Counties, rapidly dropping visibility late in the evening of Sunday, February 22nd. As the core of the still strengthening storm drew closer, winds became gusty and reduced visibility further. The combination of heavy snowfall rates and frequent wind gusts between 25 to 40 mph made for on and off blizzard conditions, with visibilities falling below one quarter of a mile, from around 3 AM through nearly 2 PM Monday, February 23, 2026 across Dutchess and eastern Ulster Counties. Snow finally began to gradually slow after 2 PM Monday, February 23, 2026 and eventually tapered off after 4 PM. The resulting snowfall totals across Dutchess and eastern Ulster Counties ranged from 7 to 18 inches.||As previously mentioned, this was a very complicated forecast. Model guidance in the days leading up to the event was highly variable in their depictions of the track and strength of the system. Ultimately, the track of the storm remained farther south and east than what was anticipated, leading to a fairly steep southeast to northwest gradient in snowfall totals. This also led to much lower snowfall totals than expected in many areas, including the immediate Capital Region, Taconic and Helderberg Mountains, Mohawk Valley, and Lake George-Saratoga Region. Outside of eastern Greene County, which ultimately received 7 to 17.5 inches of snow due to a combination of orographic enhancement and wrap around snow bands, snowfall totals within the Mid-Hudson Valley, Capital Region, Taconics, Helderbergs, Mohawk Valley, and Lake George-Saratoga Regions only amounted to about 0.3 to 6 inches.||Ahead of the event, the Governor of New York, Kathy Hochul, declared a State of Emergency for Albany, Columbia, Greene, Dutchess, Schenectady, Schoharie, and Ulster Counties in an attempt to keep residents off the roads. Consequently, many schools; local businesses; and roadways were closed, and there was a travel ban instated for all nonessential travel beginning at 9 PM on Sunday, February 22nd for Ulster and Dutchess Counties. ||Key Impacts: state of emergency, travel ban, road closures, traffic accidents, school closures, power outages.

episode_narrative: A winter storm impacted much of southeast South Carolina with significant snow accumulations on January 31st along with very cold wind chill temperatures persisting into late morning February 1st. An area of low pressure shifted off the Southeast Coast while deepening, ushering in a very cold air mass across the region. Snow accumulation ended by midnight on January 31st, but hazardous traveling conditions and very cold wind chill temperatures persisted through morning hours on February 1st.

The wind chill temperature first fell to 10 degrees or less at the Ridgeville mesonet site at 5 AM EST.

episode_narrative: Throughout February 2026, drought conditions in Maine remained stable in their classification from the USDM, maintaining extreme to severe drought conditions. By the end of the month, Maine���s drought coverage was nearly 1% Extreme Drought (D3), 53% Severe Drought (D2), and 46% Moderate Drought (D1). The freeze cap locked down any recharge to the system groundwater, while surface hydrologic conditions showed signs of continued deterioration with below normal precipitation. Precipitation during February was notably insufficient, with much of the region recording less than 50% of normal accumulations. This deficit was compounded by deep soil frost depths ranging from 6 to 20 inches, which acted as an impermeable barrier and prevented any melting snow or rain from recharging stressed aquifers. Consequently, groundwater levels in southern Maine continued to decline, reaching or falling below the historic lows observed during the 2002 drought. While snow was present across the state, the snowpack remained below normal in central and northern regions, and hundreds of households reported dry private wells due to the persistent lack of recovery.

episode_narrative: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

Forcing within the mid-levels allowed for moderate to heavy snow to fall across western MN. episode_narrative: Eastern Oklahoma experienced only one rainfall event during the month of February. During this mid-month event, rainfall across the region ranged from one hundredth to one tenth of an inch across portions of northeastern Oklahoma to as much as three to four inches across portions of east central and southeastern Oklahoma. The rainfall that fell across eastern Oklahoma in February was below the monthly average amounts for much of the region, with a large portion of northeastern Oklahoma only receiving from one to five percent of monthly average precipitation amounts. These very dry conditions, compounding on several months of dry weather, allowed the drought that developed across portions of the region in January to expand in February. Severe (D2) drought conditions developed across all of Washington, Nowata, Craig, Ottawa, Rogers, Mayes, Delaware, Wagoner, and Cherokee Counties, and developed across portions of Tulsa, Muskogee, Adair, McIntosh, Pittsburg, Pushmataha, and Choctaw Counties. Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed into portions of Choctaw, Ottawa, Delaware, Mayes, Wagoner, Cherokee, Muskogee and Adair Counties during the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

episode_narrative: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.

Following the initial onset of D2 on November 18, 2025, the county experienced a brief period of mid-winter marginal improvement before conditions degraded back to D2 levels in late January. By the end of February, the county had recorded a total of 11 weeks at or above the D2 threshold, with drought conditions persisting into March.

A potent area of low pressure stationed across southern Ontario allowed for a surface cold front to begin tracking across the Great Lake region during that afternoon and evening hours of February 6, 2026. As this cold front approached portions of central Pennsylvania, rapid drops in visibility were beginning to be observed on webcams due to snow squalls. These snow squalls continued across portions of southwestern Pennsylvania during the late evening hours of February 6th, mainly across Somerset County. As the cold front continued progressing across the region, snow showers intensity waned; however, an isolated snow squall in Schuylkill County was also observed with a rapid drop to near-zero visibility on Interstate 81. Cold air and gusty winds in the wake of the cold frontal passage allowed for dangerously cold wind chills across much of western Pennsylvania. No injuries or fatalities were reported with these snow squalls and the extreme cold that followed the cold frontal passage as temperatures began to warm during the late morning and early afternoon hours of February 7th.
event_narrative: Bitterly cold temperatures and gusty winds led to dangerously cold wind chills during the morning hours of February 7th across Elk County. The coldest wind chill observed was -27 degrees in Saint Marys during the early morning hours of February 7, 2026.

Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.

episode_narrative: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across the Ozarks but limited precipitation through the month allowed Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to develop across portions of far south central Missouri. Some expansion of drought conditions occurred through the month across portions of southwestern Missouri as well. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
event_narrative: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced continued dry conditions with drought remaining Severe (D2) drought to Moderate (D1) drought in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

episode_narrative: A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Most of these tornadoes were brief, and none were stronger than EF-1, but one serious injury occurred in Crawford County as a result of a tornado. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.

An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and development of extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across portions of Southwest Arkansas through the month of February. Rainfall amounts during February only tallied to 0.50-2.00+ inches, which was less than half of the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, extreme (D3) drought developed across Northern Howard County Arkansas by the second week of the month.

A strengthening storm system lifted through the Middle Mississippi Valley on the 19th, dragging its warm frontal zone northward through the Midwest, and bringing near-record high temperatures and anomalous dewpoints into central Indiana.  Multiple rounds of severe weather occurred over the region, from early morning large hail in two far-northern zones, covering roads in Warren County, to more organized evening severe weather from rotating supercell thunderstorms.  Through the evening of the 19th, the destabilized atmosphere combined with a stregthening low-level jet stream that progressed eastward into the region, boosting 0-1 km wind shear as high as 300 m2/s2.  A resultant cluster of discrete late-day to evening supercells were focused along the frontal zone, near or south of the Interstate 70 corridor, and produced scattered large hail over 6 counties and isolated wind damage to trees and/or power poles in 4 counties.  ||A stronger supercell with a history of producing two weak tornadoes in Crawford County, Illinois, continued into central Indiana, spawning an EF-0 tornado in Sullivan County, an intense EF-2 just west of Bloomington that caused extensive structural damage to homes, apartments, and airport facilities, and a brief EF-U in Decatur County;  this cell also produced ping-pong ball (1.50-inch diameter) sized hail in Greene and Monroe Counties.
event_narrative: An EF-U tornado tracked 0.92 miles through central Decatur County, just west of Greensburg.  The vortex's path width was 25 yards.  The tornado was identified by video footage but produced no damage.

episode_narrative: A winter storm system tracked across the West Coast, North Slope, and Interior Alaska from February 20 through February 25, 2026. The episode began with widespread blizzard conditions impacting the West Coast and North Slope regions, where powerful winds and significant blowing snow reduced visibilities to near zero. As the system pushed inland, it transitioned into a heavy snow event for the Central and Eastern Interior. Notable snowfall reports included thirteen and one-half inches measured northwest of Ester and nearly nine inches reported by storm spotters in the Tanana Valley. Additionally, measurements from the Nenana Snotel indicated a seven-inch snow depth increase over a twenty-four-hour period during the height of the storm. These conditions created hazardous travel and significant impacts to infrastructure across the state. No fatalities or injuries were reported during this episode.
event_narrative: A significant winter storm impacted the Lower Kobuk Valley, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 0431AKST on February 20 through 2059AKST on February 22, 2026. The Robert Curtis Memorial Airport AWOS (PFNO) in Noorvik first reported visibilities reduced to one-half mile in snow and freezing fog with sustained winds of twenty-nine miles per hour gusting to thirty-five miles per hour at 0739AKST on February 21. During the peak of the event, the station measured sustained winds of twenty-three miles per hour with a peak gust of thirty-five miles per hour and one-half mile visibility in snow and freezing fog. The first verifying observation for the warning occurred at 0739AKST on February 21. Hazardous conditions, including blowing snow and reduced visibilities, persisted until the warning was downgraded on February 22. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

episode_narrative: A strong Bering Sea low moves into the Gulf of Anadyr, allowing for a strong front to move into Western Alaska. As the front approached the West Coast, strong east/southeast winds brought blizzard and whiteout conditions to much of the Seward Peninsula south. A secondary push of moisture brought by a shortwave system pushed off the Bering Sea low allowed for widespread heavy snow across St. Lawrence Island, the southern Seward Peninsula, and parts of the Western Interior. As the front pushed eastward across the state, snow squalls developed over portions of the Central Interior, leading to periods of heavy snowfall and gusty winds.

Conditions were at their lowest between 14:00L on 2/19 to 17:00L on 2/19 due to snow squalls in the area.

episode_narrative: A blockbuster winter storm that impacted millions across the lower 48, bringing a combination of ice; sleet; snow; rain; and strong winds, brought widespread heavy snowfall accumulations to all of western Massachusetts from January 25-26th, 2026. ||An arctic blast made for dangerously cold conditions across western Massachusetts from January 23-24, creating a requisite cold airmass that supported snow as the primary precipitation type with this storm. The connection of the northern and southern stream flow regimes then steered a potent, Gulf-originating low pressure system to the northeast. Strong to anomalous low- to mid-level dynamics drove impressive moisture transport from the Gulf and western Atlantic in and across the region the morning of the impending storm, Sunday January 25th. Snow began Sunday morning, initially with a large dendritic growth zone courtesy of persistent arctic air being filtered into the region from northerly flow about a nearby surface high to the northeast. However, as the storm tracked closer, its associated warm nose modified the thermal profile and shrunk and lifted the dendritic growth zone into the mid and upper levels of the atmosphere by the afternoon. Snowfall rates that initially looked to reach up to 2-4 per hour within laterally translating snow bands therefore became limited to 1-2 per hour courtesy of the disconnect between the best low-level forcing and the dendritic growth zone. Still, a widespread 10-20 of snow fell across the region between Sunday, January 25th and Monday, January 26th. ||The Governor of Massachusetts, Maura Healey, declared a state of emergency prior to this event which authorized additional local resources as well as orders for travel restrictions. NWS Albany additionally received reports of numerous school and road closures in addition to traffic accidents across western Massachusetts. ||Key Impacts: state of emergency declarations, road closures, school closures, traffic accidents.

event_narrative: Minimum low temperature of -13 degrees Fahrenheit recorded with a minimum wind chill of -31 degrees Fahrenheit.

episode_narrative: A very moist and moderately unstable airmass was in place across southwest Mississippi during the morning of January 10th.  Precipitable water values were around 1.7 inches, well above the climatological 90th percentile and near record for this time of year.  A prefrontal convergence zone, enhanced by outflow boundaries and strong low-level moisture transport, supported a corridor of training showers and thunderstorms along the Louisiana/Mississippi border into southwest Mississippi. Within this environment, repeated rounds of heavy rainfall produced rain rates of 1 to 3 inches per hour. Training convection resulted in widespread rainfall totals of several inches with localized amounts approaching or exceeding a foot of rain across portions of Amite and Pike Counties over a relatively short period.  This led to widespread flash flooding, including inundated roadways, stranded vehicles, flooded structures, and rapidly rising rivers and creeks.
event_narrative: A social media post showed a creek overflowing its bank near Percy Quin State Park. The water covered a bridge that crossed the creek and a gravel driveway by several feet.

episode_narrative: An Arctic airmass entered the UP late on the 22nd, with very cold wind chills of -25F or lower persisting at times through the morning of the 26th. The coldest wind chills occurred during the mornings of the 23rd and 24th, when minimum values ranged from -30 to -55F in the central and western UP, and -25 to -25F in the eastern UP. For some areas in the central and western UP, this was the coldest 3 and 4 day stretch since January 2019. Numerous schools, businesses, and services were closed on Friday the 23rd and Saturday the 24th.||In addition to the cold temperatures, blizzard conditions accompanied the initial push of cold air during the afternoon and evening of the 22nd in the Keweenaw, with whiteout conditions leading to several traffic accidents and road closures. Another round of heavy accumulating lake effect snow occurred in the northeastern UP on the 23rd, with very low visibilities resulting in at least one road closure.
event_narrative: High winds, accumulating snow, and cold temperatures resulted in blizzard conditions during the afternoon and evening of the 22nd. US-41 was closed in at least two spots north of Houghton due to traffic accidents and whiteout conditions. There was an 8-car pileup near the Houghton County Airport, and multiple smaller accidents. Key impacts: traffic accidents, transportation delays, road closures.

episode_narrative: A significant winter storm occurred across the southern, eastern, and northeastern United States during January 23-26, 2026. A strong low pressure system moved across Baja California toward the Desert Southwest and then across the southern to northeastern portions of the country during this time frame. This low pressure system was preceded by a strong arctic cold front, which dropped surface temperatures down to record breaking lows across portions of the southern United States, including the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. Winter impacts were felt across nearly half of the country, with around an inch of freezing rain occurring at some areas across the southeastern US, inches of sleet across portions of north Texas, and up to one to two feet of snow for the Midwest into New England. This winter storm brought mostly snow to the region, but also there was some sleet mixed in across the southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle during the onset of precipitation across the region. Two to three day snow accumulation across the area ranged from just over an inch across the northwestern Panhandles to around nine to ten inches for the southeast Texas Panhandle. Frigid temperatures were also associated with this system and wind chill values dropped to as low as -20 to -25��F in the early morning hours during this time period. Temperatures remained below freezing across most of the Panhandles from early Friday morning behind the cold front passage until midday on Monday, January 26. The combination of the dangerously cold temperatures and impactful snowfall led to the closure of multiple school districts across the region as well as businesses and local government buildings. A few locations also saw infrastructure impacts such as pipes bursting in the region. Several counties also opened warming centers for the prolonged cold weather.
event_narrative: Spearman and Gruver both received an estimate two inches of snow. Overall the county observed up to two inches.

episode_narrative: A historically damaging ice storm occurred across northeast Louisiana and the surrounding region. The corridor of heaviest ice accretion, with ice thickness measured at up to one inch, spanned from Richland Parish, including the area from Rayville to Delhi, northeastward through West and East Carroll parishes and the Lake Providence area. Tree damage in this region was tremendous, and several homes were damaged or destroyed by falling trees. Travel impacts persisted through Friday, January 30th in some areas. More than 143,000 customers in Louisiana lost power during the peak of the storm with thousands of power poles broken. Full power restoration took more than two weeks in the hardest hit areas, and it took more than one week for some customers in East Carroll, Franklin, Madison, Morehouse, Richland, and West Carroll parishes. Some meters remained unpowered for three weeks in the hardest hit portions of our area. The loss of electricity and the very cold temperatures that followed resulted in the loss of water in several communities.||Significant sleet accumulations, as high as 2 in Morehouse Parish occurred over parts of the area as well. In these areas, the weight of the accumulation resulted in the collapse of several sheds, carports, gas station awnings and the roofs of some buildings. Sleet remained on the ground across much of Morehouse Parish for an entire week.||Bitter cold conditions followed the storm, with temperatures as low as 10 to 15 degrees. Note: At several area weather stations, the lowest wind chill was unavailable because the anemometer was frozen and unable to record wind speed data.||One death due to hypothermia occurred in Franklin Parish.
event_narrative: Trees and power lines were brought down in a few locations causing power outages. No road or bridge impacts were observed across the parish. Maximum freezing rain accumulations were estimated at 0.25 inches.

episode_narrative: An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. Cold temperatures (wind chill) below 30F arrived during the late evening of the 24th across the ranchlands and spread to the lower Rio Grande Valley before daybreak on the 25th.  A cold afternoon set the stage for the overnight of the 25th into the morning of the 26th, as skies cleared but fresh breezes/stronger winds near the coast prevailed.  The 26th was the coldest ambient and feels-like temperature of the calendar year so far, with a freeze in all areas, and wind chill below 20F in most areas.  ||Clear skies and calm winds allowed rapid temperature drops during the evening of the 26th, with many inland locations recording their second hard freeze in as many nights early on the 27th. Locations closer to the coast saw winds veer to the northeast above the surface, precluding a second freeze/hard freeze. ||The hard freeze caused minor damage to tender vegetation and crops in Hidalgo, Willacy, and Cameron County.  Dollar values were unknown as of this writing (end of March 2026) but some estimates are included, and will likely be updated.
event_narrative: Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport  (BRO) recorded minimum wind chill values at or below 30F degrees (Cold Weather Advisory Criteria) for 6 hours from 4:35-10:20am CST on Sunday January 25th. Harlingen/Valley International Airport (HRL) recorded minimum wind chill values at or below 30F degrees (Cold Weather Advisory Criteria) for 11.5 hours from 11:25pm (Jan 24th) to 10:40am CST January 25th.

episode_narrative: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region.||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.

By the end of February, the county had recorded a cumulative total of five weeks at or above the D2 threshold since the drought���s inception in the fall.

episode_narrative: An atmospheric river brought snow followed by high winds, warming temperatures and heavy rain to the panhandle January 8th and 9th. A low pressure center developed along a triple point front as it tracked NE across the western Gulf of Alaska on the 9th. The low center deepened to 960mb as it approached the northern Gulf and the frontal system brought a period of high winds to the central and southern panhandle. This system brought with it heavy snow across the north, followed by a significant warm-up, heavy rain, localized flooding due to previous heavy snow blocking drainages, and avalanches. The flooding falls into the advisory level, but the rain was an additional impact due to the added weight of the snow on structures. Disaster declarations were expanded to more communities across the northern panhandle after this storm.
event_narrative: Intermittent light snow fell on the 8th, becoming steady late with winds turning out of the north. Visibility fell to a half mile in the 6am hour on the 9th at the airport. A trained spotter measured 5.8 inches of snow by 7am out the road near Cohen Drive and another spotter measured 7.5 inches just before 8am. The Juneau Airport began mixing with rain around 8am while temperatures were still 30F, then fully transitioned to rain over the next 2 hours. The DOT RWIS station near Cohen Drive continued to see snow or a mix into the afternoon, then temperatures warmed above 32F at 5pm. Freezing levels rose steadily through the event, rising to around 4kft by 6pm based on the South Douglas JAWS profiler.||During the evening of the 8th, the City and Borough of Juneau announced public facilities and schools would be closed the following day due to ongoing hazardous road and weather conditions. Several small avalanches were reported during the the 9th off of Mt. Juneau, Mt. Roberts and the Thane area. No damage was reported from the avalanches and evacuation advisories and road closures were already in place. As rain fell on deep snowpack, localized flooding reports came in through the evening of the 9th particularly in Douglas, downtown Juneau, along Egan Drive, and in the Mendenhall Valley. The additional weight of snow and rain caused a vessel to sink in Douglas Harbor. This was the 11th vessel to sink in Juneau since the December record snow began. Other small out buildings and sheds succumbed to the added weight of rain on snow as well. A disaster declaration was in effect during this time.

episode_narrative: After an active period of multiple systems moving through the area bringing periods of high winds to the southern panhandle, a stronger system arrived bringing high winds to majority of the Panhandle on the 13th into the 14th. This low center tracked northward through the eastern gulf, while deepening, along with a storm force front. The low center moved onshore along the NE Gulf Coast in vicinity of Yakutat overnight Tuesday the 13th. As the low jumped inland, winds spiked up through the inner channels, lasting longest for the Skagway area.
event_narrative: Strong easterly winds with gusts of 45-55mph across the Yakutat area late on the 13th, saw a sharp wind shift out of the west in the 1am hour, spiking up to high wind. The peak wind gust measured at the Yakutat Airport ASOS was 53kt (61mph) at 248am on the 14th.

episode_narrative: Relatively clear early-day skies on February 12 led to isolated convection with rain and snow showers across portions of eastern Utah. Some valleys were already saturated or near-saturated due to periods of precipitation over the prior days. As such, in spite of dense cloud cover lingering overnight and lacking radiational cooling, saturated surface conditions paired with weakening winds were capable of producing areas of dense fog on the morning on February 13.
event_narrative: Localized dense fog developed near the eastern Uinta Mountains during the early morning of February 13. The K40U AWOS at the Manilla Airport observed reduced visibility to 1/4 mile for about twenty minutes. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

episode_narrative: A low pressure trough digging southward down the west coast along with a 180 kt jet stream allowed a significant surge of Atmospheric River moisture along with strong southwest winds to advect into eastern Utah and western Colorado. This allowed for significant mountain snowfall across most mountains in eastern Utah and western Colorado where one to two feet of snow fell. Snowfall transitioned from a heavy wet snow with lower snow ratios in the early stages to an efficient power like snow with higher snowfall ratios due to the drastically changing temperatures. Some favored southwest slopes received up to three or more feet of snow as well. The strong jet allowed for strong winds and blowing snow in addition to the heavy snow falling with gusts in the 45 to 60 mph range on average across the mountains with some localized higher gusts above 70 mph. Due to the warm airmass, most lower valleys received rain or a mix limiting accumulations except the southwest Colorado valleys that saw a combination of heavy snow and blowing snow due to the wind once they received the colder air with a second shortwave and strong cold front towards the latter half of this three day storm event.  There were also some snow squalls in some areas due to the combination of heavy snow, wind and low visibility at times with the passage of the strong cold front toward the latter half of the event.
event_narrative: Generally around 22.5 inches of snow fell at East Willow Creek in the higher elevations. Winds gusted in the 45 to 60 mph range with a peak wind gust of 59 mph at Wildhorse RAWS.

episode_narrative: A deep upper trough reinforced by a series of short waves plunging arctic air through interior North America, maintained persistent anomalous cold over central Indiana through January's final week, which was enhanced by a deep snow pack over most zones.  Temperatures from early on the 26th through the 31st most often ranged from negative single digits up to the teens to around 20 degrees, with isolated periods featuring minimum temperatures as low as -20 degrees, or maxmum temperatures as low as widespread single digits on the 26th.  Corresponding sustained winds were most often under 10 mph when resultant wind chills approached or exceeded the negative 20 degree criteria, although higher speeds of 10-20 mph occasionally occurred, especially on the 26th.  The only criteria temperature observation was in Randoph County on the morning of the 30th.||Criteria wind chills were most prevalent during both the 26th daytime and the 26-27th overnight, occurring in 22 of the region's 39 counties during both periods.  Extreme cold occurred again in 15 zones within the 28th's AM hours.  Further extreme cold was confined within the same four central to northeast central Indiana counties, during overnights of both the 28-29th and 29-30th;  although wind chill values just shy of criteria were scattered across mainly northern portions of central Indiana.  A final period of extreme cold occurred prior to dawn on February 1st in two counties.  Overall, 29 central Indiana counties observed extreme cold during at least one period, and 16 of these zones observed criteria on at least 3 periods, most often the 26th through the 28th.  Spatial distribution of extreme cold was most consistent over the region's north-central quadrant, while exhibiting a subtle trend from all west-central zones on the 26th to a few east-central zones thereafter.
event_narrative: On the 26th daytime, temperatures were as low as -3F, while breezy winds were sustained up to around 10 mph...resulting in marginally extreme wind chills as low as -20F.

episode_narrative: A major winter storm impacted eastern Kentucky from January 24 through January 25, 2026, delivering a combination of heavy snow, sleet, and significant ice accretion. The event began with heavy snow on the afternoon of the 24th, but a potent warm nose of air aloft moved over the region overnight, transitioning precipitation into a prolonged period of freezing rain and sleet for much of the area.||The most severe icing impacts occurred in the Cumberland Basin and south-central Kentucky, where significant ice accumulations up to 0.78 inches were measured. This ice loading led to significant power outages: South Kentucky RECC reported outages peaking at over 28,000 members, while Jackson Energy peaked at 12,156 members. In many areas, the weight of the ice snapped large trees and downed power lines. Restoration efforts continued through January 31 due to the scale of the damage and hazardous terrain. As the system exited on January 26, an Arctic airmass surged into the region, causing the sloppy snow, sleet, ice to freeze into a glacier-like pack that persisted into February. This led an extended period of icy roadways. With a total liquid of 1.5 to 4.0 inches, some flooding also occurred in far southeastern Kentucky where more of the precipitation fell as rain.

Additional light snow occurred on the back of the system. The combined weight downed a large tree across KY Highway 205 near Paxton at 1100EST on the 25th.

Further east, a snow squall along an Arctic front brought a quick coating in inch or snow.

episode_narrative: A very moist and moderately unstable airmass was in place across southwest Mississippi during the morning of January 10th.  Precipitable water values were around 1.7 inches, well above the climatological 90th percentile and near record for this time of year.  A prefrontal convergence zone, enhanced by outflow boundaries and strong low-level moisture transport, supported a corridor of training showers and thunderstorms along the Louisiana/Mississippi border into southwest Mississippi. Within this environment, repeated rounds of heavy rainfall produced rain rates of 1 to 3 inches per hour. Training convection resulted in widespread rainfall totals of several inches with localized amounts approaching or exceeding a foot of rain across portions of Amite and Pike Counties over a relatively short period.  This led to widespread flash flooding, including inundated roadways, stranded vehicles, flooded structures, and rapidly rising rivers and creeks.
event_narrative: A social media post showed a picture of several cars flooded along Pine Street and Douglas Drive near Higgins Middle School. The water appeared to be a couple feet deep.

episode_narrative: A significant winter storm occurred across the southern, eastern, and northeastern United States during January 23-26, 2026. A strong low pressure system moved across Baja California toward the Desert Southwest and then across the southern to northeastern portions of the country during this time frame. This low pressure system was preceded by a strong arctic cold front, which dropped surface temperatures down to record breaking lows across portions of the southern United States, including the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. Winter impacts were felt across nearly half of the country, with around an inch of freezing rain occurring at some areas across the southeastern US, inches of sleet across portions of north Texas, and up to one to two feet of snow for the Midwest into New England. This winter storm brought mostly snow to the region, but also there was some sleet mixed in across the southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle during the onset of precipitation across the region. Two to three day snow accumulation across the area ranged from just over an inch across the northwestern Panhandles to around nine to ten inches for the southeast Texas Panhandle. Frigid temperatures were also associated with this system and wind chill values dropped to as low as -20 to -25��F in the early morning hours during this time period. Temperatures remained below freezing across most of the Panhandles from early Friday morning behind the cold front passage until midday on Monday, January 26. The combination of the dangerously cold temperatures and impactful snowfall led to the closure of multiple school districts across the region as well as businesses and local government buildings. A few locations also saw infrastructure impacts such as pipes bursting in the region. Several counties also opened warming centers for the prolonged cold weather.
event_narrative: This system brought 5 to almost 10 of snow to Wheeler County. The heaviest snow fell across the southern and eastern parts of the county. Reports of 9 inches came in from Shamrock and 9.8 inches 9 miles ESE of Shamrock. Mobeetie received 8 inches of snow and Allison was estimated to have received 6 inches.

episode_narrative: Temperatures bottoming out around zero during Friday morning, coupled with wind speeds in excess of 15 mph, produced wind chills of 15 to 25 below zero across most of southeast Michigan. The arctic airmass persisted into Saturday morning, with renewed wind chill drops to around 30 degrees below zero across Midland, Saginaw, Tuscola, Genesee, Livingston, and Washtenaw counties.

episode_narrative: Broad scale upper lift led to a complex winter storm across East Tennessee, with onset precipitation of snow transitioning to freezing rain before ending as rain as the temperatures rose through the evening, night, and following morning. This storm led to 7 fatalities in East Tennessee. On the morning of the 25th the strengthening low level jet that was advancing warm air northwards led to a high end mountain wave wind event in portions of the East Tennessee mountains.
event_narrative: Two bouts of winter weather occurred in Johnson County, with the Coop observer in Mountain City reporting 2.6 inches of snowfall. Freezing rain likely occurred, but no direct measurements were reported.

episode_narrative: Broad scale upper lift led to a complex winter storm across southwestern Virginia, with onset precipitation of snow transitioning to a long period of freezing rain and icing conditions. Precipitation eventually changed over in all locations to rain. On the backside of the system another bout of light snowfall occurred.
event_narrative: A significant and highly damaging ice storm unfolded in Washington County VA as temperatures struggled to get to 32F or above, especially in the northeastern portion of the county. Ice accretion ranged from 0.25 to 0.50 inches across the county, resulting in significant damage. A trained spotter reported a maximum of 0.75 inch in the Emory and Meadowview areas, these locations stayed below freezing for a significant period of time. Extensive utility damage occurred, with power poles, powerlines, and transformers breaking from either ice weight outright or collapse of trees. At least 45% of the county was without power by the evening on the 25th. Snow and sleet accumulations of 0.8 inches near Bristol and 2.0 inches at the coop in Abingdon were also recorded.

Residential solar panels sustained damage, and several trash cans were displaced. A resident reported loud wind noise at the time of the event.

Downstream, strong surface high pressure was centered over the Midwest and Ohio Valley, promoting persistent cold air advection into the Lower Mississippi Valley and reinforcing a shallow subfreezing airmass.||Isentropic ascent intensified across the Mid-South beginning late January 23rd, as warm, moist air overran the shallow Arctic dome. Poor road conditions continued for nearly two weeks after the storm, causing difficult travel and widespread school cancellations.
event_narrative: Sleet and snow accumulations of 5 to 6 inches.

The corridor of heaviest ice accretion, with ice thickness measured at up to one inch, spanned from Richland Parish, including the area from Rayville to Delhi, northeastward through West and East Carroll parishes and the Lake Providence area. Tree damage in this region was tremendous, and several homes were damaged or destroyed by falling trees. Travel impacts persisted through Friday, January 30th in some areas. More than 143,000 customers in Louisiana lost power during the peak of the storm with thousands of power poles broken. Full power restoration took more than two weeks in the hardest hit areas, and it took more than one week for some customers in East Carroll, Franklin, Madison, Morehouse, Richland, and West Carroll parishes. Some meters remained unpowered for three weeks in the hardest hit portions of our area. The loss of electricity and the very cold temperatures that followed resulted in the loss of water in several communities.||Significant sleet accumulations, as high as 2 in Morehouse Parish occurred over parts of the area as well. In these areas, the weight of the accumulation resulted in the collapse of several sheds, carports, gas station awnings and the roofs of some buildings. Sleet remained on the ground across much of Morehouse Parish for an entire week.||Bitter cold conditions followed the storm, with temperatures as low as 10 to 15 degrees. Note: At several area weather stations, the lowest wind chill was unavailable because the anemometer was frozen and unable to record wind speed data.||One death due to hypothermia occurred in Franklin Parish.
event_narrative: Ice accumulation was observed in trees and on powerlines. Highest accumulations of 0.25 inches were observed the Northern parts of the parish. Bridges had a layer of ice. Central and southern portions had less accumulation.

episode_narrative: A prolonged period of winter weather affected South Texas during the final week of January 2026, beginning with the arrival of a strong Arctic front early on January 24. The front surged southward faster than initially anticipated, producing a rapid temperature drop across the region and widespread rain behind the boundary. As colder air deepened overnight, precipitation continued while temperatures approached or fell below freezing across parts of the region, creating a narrow window for freezing rain and drizzle late January 24 into the morning of January 25. The greatest risk for ice accumulation occurred across the Victoria Crossroads, where light ice totals of up to around a tenth of an inch were possible. Elsewhere, the combination of lingering precipitation and wet roadways raised concerns for patchy black ice, particularly on bridges and overpasses as temperatures briefly dipped to freezing.||Once the precipitation ended on January 25, the primary hazard transitioned to extreme cold as a deep Arctic air mass settled over South Texas. Temperatures struggled to rise above the 40s during the day, while overnight lows dropped into the teens across northern inland areas and the lower to mid-20s closer to the coast. Persistent northerly winds produced dangerously low wind chills, with values falling into the single digits in some inland locations and the teens elsewhere. Extreme Cold Warnings and Freeze Warnings were issued across the region as the prolonged cold posed risks to infrastructure, agriculture, and vulnerable populations. Clearer skies and lighter winds early in the week allowed efficient radiational cooling, reinforcing the cold conditions through January 27 before gradual moderation began.||Although temperatures slowly recovered into the 50s and 60s by midweek, the pattern remained active with additional frontal passages. A brief warmup ahead of another cold front late in the week pushed temperatures into the 70s before colder air returned by January 30. This secondary surge brought another round of below-freezing temperatures and widespread cold weather headlines, particularly across inland counties where lows fell into the 20s and wind chills dropped into the teens. While precipitation with this second front remained limited, the extended period of repeated freezes and persistent cold made this late-January event a notable winter episode for South Texas.
event_narrative: Extreme Cold/Wind Chill: KVCT reported wind chills at or below 15 degF for at least 2 hours, which is our local Extreme Cold Warning criteria.
